Overview
Sahl helps people manage all their household payments in one place. The goal was to turn a fragmented payment landscape into one seamless experience that saves time and reduces anxiety.
The problem: Inconsistent service flows and overwhelming navigation caused high drop-off and confusion. The existing system couldn’t scale with Sahl’s growing list of services.
My role: I designed a consistent navigation pattern and a set of reusable components the team could scale with, working with one other designer, and a PM.
About Sahl

200+ services ·
#1 fintech app in Egypt

Strategy Board
These were the targets we set going in — not results we claim.
Problem
Fragmented dropdowns and inconsistent first screens across 200+ service flows created confusion and high drop-off.
Objective
Standardize the user journey and unify navigation logic for all household payments, while supporting rapid service expansion.
Customer Segment
Existing Sahl users and new digital adopters in Egypt looking for simpler payment experiences.
Success Measure
Less first-screen drop-off and faster time-to-action for top services.
Goals
Fewer user errors, fewer Customer Success tickets, faster implementation cycles, more user confidence.
Research
I worked from three sources: ongoing collaboration with Customer Success (recurring complaints, edge cases, friction moments), competitor analysis, and usability observations.

Key finding — navigation and provider identification: Services used inconsistent first-screen logic and long text-only dropdowns. Without visual cues like logos, users struggled to identify providers, leading to wrong selections and early exits.
The resulting pattern: logo-first selection, alphabetical ordering, searchable lists — one navigation pattern across 200+ services, fewer selection errors.
Sitemap

The map covered every entry point into the app: sign in/sign up, and every service category beneath it — mobile, internet, landline, gaming, education, donations, and general bills. For each, I traced the full payment path down to the final screen, and kept a separate log of error states and edge cases alongside a running notes sheet of insights worth solving systemically rather than fixing one flow at a time.
Sitemap of the entire app before any changes.
Wireframes & Early Concepts
I sketched three core patterns before touching high fidelity:
Bundle purchase: mobile → operator → service → choose bundle
Top-up: mobile → operator → top-up type → amount → pay
Bill enquiry: mobile → operator → bills → bill info → select bill(s) → pay

I also explored a separate donations flow (search/recents/full list → selected cause → pay) and tested an alternate NFC-based top-up path for smart meters, flagging open questions directly on the sketches — like whether to auto-select a service when there was only one option, or drop unnecessary fields depending on the entry point.
Some wireframes sketching out all services and their shared solutions.
Scaling the pattern: Donations, Education & Gaming

Donations, Education, and Gaming vouchers all suffered from the same core problem as telecom — long text-only dropdowns, no visual cues, and anxiety at the payment step. So all three got the same treatment, built from the same components:
Giving meant a phone-number field and one long text dropdown of charities — no logos, no search, no discovery.

Three ways in. Recents — "Donate Again" repeats a frequent contribution in a single tap, removing friction from habit-based giving. Spotlight — prominent placement for urgent and seasonal causes, like Ramadan Iftar campaigns, that adapts to what the moment needs. All — every charity, logo-first, searchable, alphabetical.
After: Recents with one-tap "Donate Again,"Spotlight for urgent and seasonal causes like Ramadan Iftar, and a searchable logo-first list of all charities.
Education Services: New
Education: searchable institution list, student-ID guidance in-flow, details confirmed before payment.
Gaming Vouchers: New
Gaming: legible voucher codes, mandatory store selection, redemption guide built into the flow.
After: Recents with one-tap "Donate Again," Spotlight for urgent and seasonal causes like Ramadan Iftar, and a searchable logo-first list of all charities.
Telecom Services
The Problem

Telecom covers mobile, landline, and internet. Each has up to 5 providers (Vodafone, Orange, e& (Etisalat), WE, Nour), and each provider offers different payment types. Every service started on a different first screen.
Every step needed its own screen, with noticeable loading in between
Internet used a different structure than mobile
Landline asked users to pick an operator when only one existed
The Solution
Logo-first selection: Searchable, alphabetical, logo-based provider lists.
Dynamic content: Payment types appear based on the selected provider.
Consistent UX: The same interaction pattern across all telecom services.
The Impact
Fewer re-entries during provider selection
Fewer steps to complete a payment
Less confusion through instant provider recognition
Faster provider lookup through search
Telecom Services: Old
Telecom Services: New
New mobile navigation flow, also applies to the rest of the Telecom services (Landline and Internet)
Design System & Scalability
I moved the team from ad-hoc UI to a structured design language, so new services could launch using standard components.
Long-list navigation: Alphabetical, searchable, logo-first lists for large provider directories.
Recall Card: A verification component used across most services to prevent errors at the final step.
Info cards: In-flow guidance that helps users find IDs and meter numbers.
Data collection rules: Unified input validation and formatting across all service types.
The Recall Card It reduces refund and reversal requests by catching errors before payment is confirmed, and it's used across telecom, utilities, education, and donations.
Real-Time Validation
Distinguishes ambiguous characters (1/l, 0/O) in vouchers and requires regional store selection to prevent redemption errors.
Identity Confirmation
Info cards guide users to their student ID, and searchable lists replace complex dropdowns for 15+ institutions.
Friction as a Feature
An intentional pause for verification that prevents costly reversals and builds user confidence.
Recall Card: present in every flow
Outcome
Scalability: Rigid, hard-coded flows became dynamic, searchable structures ready for rapid growth.
Trust: Anxiety-inducing inputs became verified transactions with fewer errors, through the Recall Card.
Efficiency: Clear self-serve navigation helped reduce the load on support.
By the numbers: 1 navigation pattern and 4 standardized user flows across 200+ services, 80+ providers, 15+ institutions.
A note on measurement: As an early-stage startup, we had limited analytics in place, so impact reflects Customer Success feedback and the funnel signals we could gather.

/project/mascot.x: A Face for Fintech
From research to character: building a mascot people could trust
Role
Character strategy and original concept
Duration
Aug 2023 – May 2024 · Launched Jul 2025
Company
Sahl
Skills
Character Design
Brand
Overview

Sahl makes household payments easy — but easy only matters if people trust you. In Egypt’s fintech market, the hardest users to win are the ones who need the product most: lower-income, less tech-literate customers who are understandably wary of trusting a new app with their money.
The Problem
Sahl needed a recognizable, friendly face — something to humanize a technical service and build familiarity across marketing and, eventually, the product itself.
My Role

I initiated the mascot research, built the character strategy, and designed the original concept — chosen from three designers’ visions — then developed it through v3 before handing visual refinement to our team’s illustrator.
Process
Research → Strategy → Character → Visual design → Rollout plan
Why a Mascot

I started with research: how mascots work in B2C versus B2B, and close studies of two companies doing it well. Salesforce built an entire mascot family, each character fronting a product or community. Hootsuite’s Owly became the relatable voice of the social media managers who actually use the tool.

That raised our key strategic question: one mascot or many? Sahl serves both consumers and businesses, but we were still a young brand — multiple characters would confuse before they could connect. We chose one mascot who could wear different hats per context: the same face on a koshk poster, a LinkedIn post, and in your app.
The proposal went through our design lead, then the marketing manager, then a C-level presentation. All three approved.
Building The Character

Before any drawing, we defined who this character is. Each designer on the team drafted the traits that made sense to them; we merged them into one foundation. Fast, empathetic, innovative. Three values: time, people, innovation. A signature object: a lightning-bolt button on his robotic arm, tying him to Sahl’s logo. Even his fears mapped to product promises — crowds and downtime, the exact things Sahl exists to eliminate.
His working name was Ra3d — thunder, to Sahl’s lightning.
From Sketch to Budz
Each of the three designers on the team sketched their own vision for the character. Mine was chosen as the direction, and I developed it from the first sketch through v3.

We had set clear visual principles early: simple shapes, two to three colors, a silhouette you’d recognize anywhere. My drafts established the direction but weren’t fully landing those principles. Fatma ElQady , the strongest illustrator on our team, took over from v4 and drove them home — the final Budz is rounder, simpler, and friendlier, and it’s what finally cleared the marketing approval round and then C-level, with further refinements deliberately parked for a future rebrand cycle, the way any company iterates on its brand.
Defining what success looked like, then recognizing whose craft would get us there, was the job.
Evolution: Sketch → v1 → v2 → v3
Final Budz illustration
Launch & Rollout

Development wrapped in mid-2024, but the public launch waited until July 2025 — revenue-critical campaigns took priority for a small startup marketing team, and the mascot could wait. Startup prioritization in practice.

The launch was an animated origin story produced with an agency and published across Sahl’s socials. Since then, Budz fronts Instagram , Facebook , TikTok , and LinkedIn in both stills and reels, joined the company’s new event booth, and made his first in-app appearance on the loading screen.

I moved from the marketing team to the product team in June 2024; the team carried the rollout forward roughly on the plan I’d set — model sheet, expressions library, print and swag, storyboard, launch video, and in-app presence.
Final Budz illustration
Sitemap of the entire app before any changes.
Budz in the wild: Sahl social content. Produced by the Sahl marketing team.
By The Numbers
(public platform counts, September 2026)
Launch film: ~600K views across platforms — 286.8K on TikTok, 230K on Instagram, 82K on Facebook
On TikTok and Instagram, that’s roughly 7× the follower count of each account — the film reached well beyond Sahl’s existing audience
The launch film remains Budz’s best-performing content to date

An honest read: Since launch, Budz appears at seasonal moments — Eid, new year — and on Sahl’s event booth, while day-to-day content leans on real people. That’s a lighter presence than the always-on character in my original plan, and it’s the real lesson of the project: a mascot isn’t an asset, it’s a content system. What I’d push for next is the expressions library and ready-to-use templates that make Budz cheap to deploy — so he becomes part of Sahl’s daily voice rather than an occasional guest.
The goal I set for him still stands: a lighthearted guide who bridges the gap between new-to-fintech users and a product asking for their trust.
